name: Ishoku hada

lead: Ishoku hada (異色肌, roughly 'unique skin' or 'remarkable skin') is a style in which people cover their skin in body paint in colours that no natural complexion has, to look like characters from anime, games and films. It grew out of gyaru fashion and was noted in Japanese and English-language media in 2017.
Its appearance payoff is a deliberate, stylised look: painted skin combined with multicoloured wigs, bright contact lenses and accessories. Coverage described it as niche rather than mainstream.

paras: Participants use stage make-up or body paint in colours such as orange, pink, grey, yellow, aqua or purple. One participant told Kotaku that full-body painting took about three hours and that she needed help with her back. Looks are completed with wigs, coloured lenses and accessories.

Body paint and stage make-up are cosmetic products that can irritate skin; coverage did not discuss health effects. Kotaku noted that black paint could be read as offensive in the West because of blackface history, though that was not the participants' intent.

angle.text: Body paint changes how the skin looks immediately, so the wearer matches a fictional character or a chosen colour palette. The look is a costume-like fashion statement rather than a skincare or health change.

lead: Ishoku hada, written 異色肌 and translated as 'unique skin' or 'remarkable skin', is a Japanese fashion trend in which people colour their skin with body paint to resemble fantastical characters from anime, manga, films and video games.[1][2] Participants pair the paint with multicoloured wigs, bright contact lenses and colourful accessories.[1]

The look was brought to wider attention in mid-2017 by Japanese model and DJ Miyako, who was already a fan of ganguro and gyaru fashion.[1] Kotaku reported that she organised a shoot with friends at a bar in Tokyo's Kabukicho, each painted a different colour, and that the style resembles the early-2000s yamanba look.[2]
Media described it as a niche street style and a form of self-expression and unconventional beauty rather than a mass movement.[1][2]

paras: The look covers the skin with paint in shades 'all the colours of the rainbow and more', and is meant to recreate magical or alien characters.[1] Inspirations named by participants in Kotaku's coverage include Phantasy Star Online 2, Panty & Stocking's Scanty, Avatar and Marvel's Mystique.[2]

SoraNews24 reported on 5 July 2017 that the trend had appeared online the previous month, with posts from Miyako in May and June, and that fans were posting under the hashtag #異色肌ギャル.[1] Kotaku described the shoot at American Bar and Cafe Ren in Kabukicho, with participants including Miku, Sonorama and Cherry Sunaga, and said Egg magazine covered and promoted the look and that mainstream outlets such as Huffington Post Japan had begun reporting on it.[2] Fan art of the participants followed.[1][2]
Participants used stage make-up or body paint in colours such as orange, pink, grey, yellow, aqua and purple.[2] Miku said full-body coverage took around three hours and needed help for the back.[2]

Both outlets called the trend niche and said it had not yet become a mainstream subculture.[1][2] Kotaku noted that black paint could be seen as offensive in Western contexts because of blackface history, though that was not the intent of the participants.[2]

timeline.event: Miyako's posts and a Kabukicho photo shoot bring ishoku hada into online and media attention.[1][2]
